det_01.label: The dataset: a Wikidata founder→company edge list
det_01.content: This dataset was built on 2026-05-24 by querying the free Wikidata SPARQL endpoint for every entity 'founded by' (P112) a person who was 'educated at' (P69) Stanford University (Q41506). The result is an edge list of 545 founder→company links covering 394 distinct Stanford-alumni founders and 509 unique organizations across 149 industries. It is a deliberately broad net: 'founded by' captures not just companies but foundations, PACs, schools, and research institutes, and 'educated at Stanford' makes no distinction between a degree-holder and someone who enrolled for two days. The data is a map of what Stanford people have started, not a curated honor roll.

det_02.label: Frederick Terman engineered the pipeline
det_02.content: Stanford did not become a founder factory by accident. Frederick Terman (1900-1982), Dean of Engineering from 1944 and Provost from 1955, is widely called the 'father of Silicon Valley'. In the 1930s he began urging Stanford engineers to start companies near campus instead of leaving for the established East Coast electronics industry. His most famous protégés were two students named Bill Hewlett and David Packard, whom he encouraged to commercialize their work. In 1951 Terman created the Stanford Industrial Park, leasing university land to high-tech firms (Varian, HP, Kodak, GE, Lockheed) and turning the mid-Peninsula into the hotbed that became Silicon Valley. The university-to-startup pipeline this dataset measures is the direct legacy of a deliberate institutional strategy.

det_03.label: HP (1939): the original Stanford garage startup
det_03.content: Hewlett-Packard was incorporated in January 1939 in a rented garage at 367 Addison Avenue in Palo Alto. Both founders, William Hewlett and David Packard, were Stanford engineering students under Terman's mentorship. The HP Garage is officially designated the 'Birthplace of Silicon Valley' and is a California Historical Landmark. In this dataset HP is the earliest unambiguous tech-company founding and the template every later Stanford startup follows: two classmates, a garage, university encouragement, a global company.

det_04.label: Sun and Cisco were literally built on campus
det_04.content: Two of the most iconic Stanford companies were born from the university's own computer infrastructure. Sun Microsystems, founded in February 1982 by Stanford grad students Scott McNealy, Andy Bechtolsheim, and Vinod Khosla (with Berkeley's Bill Joy), took its name as a pun on SUN = Stanford University Network; Bechtolsheim's founding hardware was a workstation he designed from spare parts in the Computer Science Department. Cisco Systems grew out of Stanford campus networking work in the early 1980s, its router software descended from NOS written by Stanford's William Yeager, later the basis of Cisco's IOS. These were not companies founded by Stanford alumni who happened to study there — they were spun directly out of Stanford labs.

det_05.label: Stanford alumni founded a top-10-economy's worth of revenue
det_05.content: The scale of the Stanford entrepreneurial machine is staggering. A 2011 Stanford alumni survey found roughly 39,900 active companies founded by Stanford alumni, generating more than $2.7 trillion in annual revenue and 5.4 million jobs since the 1930s — output roughly equivalent to the world's 10th-largest economy at the time. Public giants founded by Stanford people include Google, HP, Cisco, and NVIDIA. This 545-row dataset is a tiny, Wikidata-notable slice of that universe, but it captures the spine: the household-name companies that built Silicon Valley.

det_06.label: 'Educated at Stanford' is loose — the Elon Musk problem
det_06.content: Wikidata's P69 'educated at' makes no distinction between graduates, dropouts, and brief enrollees. The starkest case is Elon Musk, who tops this dataset's founder ranking with 15 entries: Musk entered a Stanford physics PhD program in 1995 and, by widely repeated account, dropped out after about two days to chase the internet boom, launching Zip2. He is counted identically to Larry Page and Sergey Brin, who actually pursued PhDs at Stanford and built Google there. Any claim that someone is a 'Stanford founder' should be read as 'Wikidata lists them as educated at Stanford', which can mean a two-day enrollment as easily as a doctorate.

det_07.label: 'Founded by' includes non-companies — read the rankings carefully
det_07.content: The Wikidata P112 'founded by' relation attaches to any organization, not just companies. As a result the most prolific 'founders' in this dataset have entries that are really foundations, prizes, PACs, and schools. Elon Musk's 15 include America PAC, the America Party, and Astra Nova School; Peter Thiel's 10 include the Thiel Fellowship and The Stanford Review (a student newspaper); Herbert Hoover's 6 are almost entirely relief commissions and institutes from his pre/post-presidency. The honest reading is 'things Stanford alumni founded', and to count real companies you must filter out the civic and philanthropic entries.

det_08.label: The tech flag is a floor, not a ceiling
det_08.content: The dataset's is_tech flag is a keyword match on Wikidata's industry (P452) field — but 323 of the 545 links have no industry recorded at all. So the 104 rows flagged tech are a hard undercount: famous tech firms with a blank industry field (and there are many) are silently excluded. The analyst should treat is_tech as a lower bound and, where precision matters, identify tech companies by name rather than trusting the flag. The 'unspecified' industry bucket (323 rows) is by far the largest 'category' in the data and is an artifact of Wikidata coverage, not a real sector.

det_09.label: Geography: the founding clusters around Palo Alto
det_09.content: Headquarters in the dataset cluster tightly in the San Francisco Bay Area: San Francisco (60), Mountain View (24), Palo Alto (19), Sunnyvale (10), Menlo Park (10), San Jose (9), Santa Clara (5). This is the geographic signature of the Terman strategy — Stanford alumni overwhelmingly start their companies within a few miles of campus, reinforcing the local agglomeration that became Silicon Valley. New York City (11) and Washington, D.C. (9) are the largest non-Bay-Area clusters, the latter inflated by Herbert Hoover's government and relief organizations.
